# One global geometric cell: compatible positive-rate convex lifts

This is a conditional STRUCTURAL theorem about one actual global affine
cell at one fixed positive rate. Its hypotheses are explicit prelimit
slice hypotheses. It neither splits a geometric-group cap inequality
among cells nor moves the existing source anchor to a new center.

The central new fact is that a common slice normalization preserves
Brunn--Minkowski across integer fibers. An interior integer base then
forces all positive limiting fibers onto one affine graph with one
continuous tangent space. Residual density powers give a genuine lower
continuous-dimensional mixed convex lift.

## 1. Prelimit setting and simultaneous slice limits

Fix integers n>=0 and N>=1. Let P be a finite subset of Z^n. For each j
let D_j be a compact convex subset of R^n x R^D, and let

    A_j(z,x)=a_j+b_j dot z+c_j dot x,   c_j != 0,
    T_j={A_j=s_j}.

Assume that every nonempty integer fiber of D_j lies over P. All D_j
lie in one fixed compact set. The actual application has D=d and
N=d-1: D_j is ONE GLOBAL active cell of the canonical body, and T_j is
the common rate level of its active affine plane. Its slices have
continuous dimension N and parallel tangent c_j-perpendicular.

More generally, assume that these fiber slices lie in parallel
N-dimensional affine planes, with the same isometric N-volume
normalization at every base. For a scalar alpha_j>0 independent of z put

    mu_j,z=alpha_j H_N restricted to (D_j intersect T_j)_z.       (1)

Assume simultaneous finite weak convergence mu_j,z -> mu_z for every
z in P. Empty slices have zero measure. Every limiting measure is compactly
supported. Let

    P_*={z in P:mu_z is nonzero},   B=conv(P_*).

Assume P_* is nonempty. The actual inverse-volume coarea normalization is

    alpha_j=1/(M_j lambda_j |c_j|),                            (2)

with ONE global M_j, rate scale lambda_j, and continuous gradient c_j.
Using separately normalized fiber measures would destroy the argument.

For the lift theorem below also assume:

    dim aff(supp mu_z) <= N-1 for every z in P_*.                (3)

For positive-rate defects on canonical zero faces, reciprocal
integrability gives (3) with N=d-1. The proof of (3) is in
zero-face-lattice-projection-and-continuous-rank-drop-rate-geometry.md.
It is not a general assertion about arbitrary slice limits.

## 2. Joint measure Brunn--Minkowski survives the limit

For finitely many positive weights theta_i of sum one, bases z_i in P_*,
and an integer base z=sum theta_i z_i, one has z in P_* and, for compact
sets E_i of positive mu_z_i mass,

    mu_z(sum theta_i E_i)^(1/N)
       >= sum theta_i mu_z_i(E_i)^(1/N).                      (4)

In particular P_* = B intersect Z^n.

First prove the prelimit inequality whenever all input sets have positive
mu_j,z_i mass. The sets E_i intersect (D_j intersect T_j)_z_i lie in
parallel N-planes. Their weighted Minkowski sum lies in the output slice
by convexity of D_j and affinity of A_j. The ordinary N-dimensional
Brunn--Minkowski inequality gives (4) for mu_j: the common multiplier
alpha_j cancels with the same power on both sides.

Here are the weak-limit details. Given compact E_i of positive limit
mass, replace each by its open epsilon-neighborhood. Portmanteau gives
the required lower bounds for the input masses; for large j they are
positive. The output Minkowski sum lies in the closed 2epsilon-
neighborhood of the compact set E=sum theta_i E_i. Applying prelimit
Brunn--Minkowski there and then the upper Portmanteau bound for this
closed neighborhood gives

    mu_z(E+2epsilon closed ball)^(1/N)
       >= sum theta_i mu_z_i(E_i)^(1/N).

Let epsilon decrease to zero, using finiteness and continuity from above.
If an integer output base was not in P, its prelimit measure was zero,
contradicting this positive bound. Thus every integer convex combination
of positive bases lies in P and has positive limiting mass. Every integer
point of B has such a finite convex representation, proving lattice
completeness and (4).

Taking all z_i equal proves positive N-concavity of each mu_z. The fully
proved density lemma in
candidate 0798d34d2fb14df0
therefore applies. Write S_z=supp(mu_z), a compact convex set, and
q_z=dim aff(S_z). If q_z>0, mu_z=g_z H_q_z, with no relative boundary
mass and a positive finite continuous interior density satisfying

    g_z^(1/(N-q_z)) is concave.                              (5)

For q_z=0, mu_z is one positive atom.

## 3. A stronger consequence: homothetic measure domination

Fix an instance of (4), an index i, and support points x_l in S_z_l
for l != i. Define

    F_i(x)=theta_i x+sum_(l != i) theta_l x_l.

Then, as finite measures on the ambient continuous space,

    mu_z >= theta_i^N (F_i)_# mu_z_i.                       (6)

To prove this, fix a compact E of positive mu_z_i mass. For every other
index use S_z_l intersect the closed epsilon-ball at x_l, which has
positive mass. Apply (4), discarding all terms except its ith term.
The resulting compact Minkowski sums decrease, as epsilon decreases,
to F_i(E). Continuity from above gives

    mu_z(F_i(E)) >= theta_i^N mu_z_i(E).

Since F_i is an injective affine homothety, compact inner regularity
extends this inequality to every Borel set in its image, and then to
the full measure statement (6). Equivalently, first apply the compact
inequality to F_i inverse of a compact target set. No differentiation
argument or interchange of null sets is needed.

The support of the right side is F_i(S_z_i), hence it lies in S_z.
Consequently q_z_i<=q_z. On the other hand, if q_z_i<q_z, the absolutely
continuous measure mu_z gives the smaller affine space F_i(aff S_z_i)
zero mass, contradicting (6). This also covers atoms. Thus

    q_z_i=q_z and tangent(S_z_i)=tangent(S_z)                (7)

for every positive-weight input. Their affine hulls transform into the
same output affine hull under F_i.

This is stronger and simpler than a comparison of small-ball exponents.
It applies only when the WHOLE cross-fiber inequality (4) is available.

## 4. An interior integer base gives one affine physical graph

Suppose B has a relative-interior integer point z0. By lattice
completeness z0 is in P_*. It can be expressed as a convex combination
of ALL points of P_* with strictly positive weights. Indeed the average
of these points lies in relint B; use a small positive multiple of this
average and express the remaining point of B as a convex combination.
Apply (7) to this combination. All S_z have one common dimension q<N
and one common tangent space V of dimension q.

Let

    D=conv union_(z in P_*) ({z} x S_z).                    (8)

For every integer z in B,

    D_z=S_z.                                               (9)

The nontrivial inclusion follows from (4) at the level of supports.
Every convex combination of support points lies in the target support:
apply (4) to arbitrarily small positive-mass balls at the input points.
Every point of D_z is such a finite combination. Points from the same
fiber may be combined first because S_z is convex.

The vertical kernel W of aff(D) has dimension q. To verify this without
a hidden genericity assumption, take any y in relint D. Its base is
in relint B. Because z0 lies in relint B, it is a strict convex
combination of this base and another point of B. Combining y with a
point of D over that second base yields a point of relint D over z0:
the relative ball about y is scaled by a positive factor. Therefore
D_z0 has affine hull equal to the full vertical fiber of aff(D), whose
tangent is W. By (9), dim W=q. Every S_z already has tangent V, so W=V.

It follows that the V-perpendicular coordinate of every point in D is
an AFFINE function b(z) of the base z. One way to see this is to quotient
aff(D) by its vertical kernel V: projection to aff(B) is now an affine
bijection. Choose the unique representative in V-perpendicular. Thus

    S_z is contained in b(z)+V for every z in P_*.           (10)

The map x -> x-b(z) is an affine shear in the continuous coordinates.
It leaves all integer bases unchanged, preserves H_q on each fiber,
and sends physical affine halfspaces to affine halfspaces. Arbitrary
ambient affine normalization is not being used.

## 5. Residual density radii are compatible across all integer fibers

Set r=N-q>=1. If q>0 let f_z=g_z^(1/r) in relint S_z and let fbar_z
be its finite upper-semicontinuous concave extension to S_z. The
extension and its boundedness are proved in the individual-lift note.
For q=0, define fbar_z=mu_z(S_z)^(1/N) at its single point.

For every positive-weight integer-base combination as in (4), and
arbitrary x_i in S_z_i, one has

    fbar_z(sum theta_i x_i) >= sum theta_i fbar_z_i(x_i).    (11)

For q=0 this is exactly (4) for the singletons. For q>0 first take all
x_i in their relative interiors. They lie in parallel q-planes with
the common tangent V. Balls of radii epsilon a_i about them lie in
their supports for sufficiently small epsilon, and their weighted
Minkowski sum is the q-ball of radius epsilon sum theta_i a_i about
x=sum theta_i x_i. In particular x is in relint S_z. Divide (4) by
the common q-ball volume factor and use continuity of all densities:

    g_z(x) (sum theta_i a_i)^q
       >= (sum theta_i g_z_i(x_i)^(1/N) a_i^(q/N))^N.       (12)

Under the normalization sum theta_i a_i=1, Holder's inequality, with
equality at a_i proportional to g_z_i(x_i)^(1/r), evaluates the maximum
of the right side as (sum theta_i g_z_i(x_i)^(1/r))^r.
This proves (11) on relative interiors. Approximate arbitrary boundary
points by interior sequences attaining the defining upper limits of
fbar_z_i. Upper semicontinuity of the output extension gives (11) on
all supports.

Notice that (11) includes arbitrary finite convex combinations with
integer resulting base, not merely midpoint combinations or one parity.
It is inherited from the single global cell.

## 6. A genuine mixed convex body in continuous dimension N

Identify V isometrically with R^q. Define, over each z in P_*,

    K_z={(v,u) in R^q x R^r:
          b(z)+v in S_z,
          |u| <= fbar_z(b(z)+v)/omega_r^(1/r)}.             (13)

Here v denotes its isometric vector in V. Each K_z is a compact
N-dimensional convex body, including the q=0 case of a Euclidean
N-ball. Its projection under (v,u)->b(z)+v sends ordinary N-volume
exactly to mu_z. Relative boundary values of fbar do not change that
identity; the original measures give that boundary zero mass.

Equation (11) and the triangle inequality imply

    sum theta_i K_z_i is contained in K_z                 (14)

whenever the resulting base z is integer. Consequently the convex
body

    K=conv union_(z in P_*) ({z} x K_z)                    (15)

has EXACTLY K_z as its integer fibers and has no other integer fibers.
Its base projection is B, P_*=B intersect Z^n, and (14) excludes extra
points in its sampled fibers. It has affine dimension k+N, where
k=dim B: its bases span k dimensions and every fiber has N-dimensional
interior.

For precision in a lower-dimensional integer projection, translate by
an integer base point and use a lattice basis of

    span(B-B) intersect Z^n.

This saturated rank-k lattice gives integer coordinates Z^k on aff B.
The resulting K is a convex body in R^k x R^N with the standard
mixed-integer fibers K_z. No determinant from this base-coordinate
choice changes continuous N-volume.

There is one AFFINE physical projection

    (z,v,u) -> (z,b(z)+v)                                  (16)

which sends its mixed-integer volume to sum_z mu_z. Thus every original
physical closed halfspace pulls back to a closed affine halfspace;
if the pullback functional is constant and the halfspace contains a
selected point, it contains the entire support. A point in K intersect
(Z^k x R^N) projects to a point in an actual support S_z.

This is a valid route for applying a theorem already established in
continuous dimension N=d-1 to THIS one-cell, fixed-rate measure. It is
not a proof of such an inductive theorem, and the resulting point has
no proved relation to an existing source anchor or selected cap menu.

## 7. Scope of the interior-base hypothesis and remaining mixtures

If B has no relative-interior integer point, one cannot simply invoke
Section 4. The maximal minimal-face construction in
candidate 1d07780671b93642
covers its integer points by faces Q with an interior integer point
relative to Q. Restricting (4) to bases on ONE such Q preserves the
inequality and lattice completeness, and Sections 4--6 apply there.
Different Q may overlap on sampled boundary bases. These lifts are a
COVER, not a partition; summing their masses or cap credits would
double-count those fibers.

Even in the non-hollow case the theorem is for ONE global active cell.
Two global cells can belong to the same limiting affine-plane group
and have fixed-rate measures with disconnected union of supports.
The exact example in
candidate 6090c7ee45c2de64
shows this already in n=0,d=3. Such a sum cannot be a marginal of
uniform volume on one convex body. Nor may one split aggregate critical
cap-payment inequalities into cell-specific inequalities without an
additional argument.

Finally, no source anchor was used in the proof of this structural lift.
The common rate and common coarea factor in (1)--(2) are indispensable.
The actual existence of simultaneous finite limits, the zero-face rank
bound, the treatment of delayed cell starts, and compatibility with the
full marked cap law must be checked in the rate framework before this
lift is used there.
